text: Is it the case that knowledge is produced only by the material cause that is itself accompanied by the absence of defect, or is knowledge produced solely by material cause without any accompanying defect? The former—knowledge arising from material cause together with the absence of defect—is the view upheld by the proponents of the Pramāṇavāda school; the latter is not accepted. Because the material cause is accompanied by the absence of defect, the proof of the material cause’s being co‑existent with the effect is established in a way that differs from the proof of the effect’s existence by mere conjunction; this is due to the “diamond‑like” (vajra) nature of the causal relation, which is inseparable from the absence of defect. If, however, the absence itself were only a cause, then one would have to say that the absence has operative efficacy; but if the absence has no efficacy, then the continual destruction of the vessel (the “vessel‑destruction” argument) shows that the vessel’s permanence is not linked to any lasting cause.
